messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 44

He is 46, a South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life running toward danger. Before he becomes a firefighter, he volunteers as a relief worker in a war zone in his late twenties, joining a medical and supply team that moves between shelled neighborhoods, camps, and damaged hospitals. At the time, he tells himself he is good in chaos. He learns how to carry water, bandages, children, and bodies with the same steady arms. He learns how to keep moving when the ground shakes. What he does not allow himself to learn is how afraid he is.

One afternoon, the convoy he is traveling with is hit. He remembers the sound first—an impact so sharp it seems to split the air open—followed by the heavy rain of debris on metal. The truck in front of them burns fast. He sees one of the local drivers stumble out with his clothes on fire. He still remembers the man’s hands, opening and closing as if trying to catch something invisible. There are civilians nearby, including a girl he had seen earlier that morning holding a dented pot in a bread line. By the time he reaches them, there is screaming everywhere, then a strange silence in his own head. He moves automatically, dragging one person, then another, pressing cloth into wounds, shouting for supplies. He is certain at several moments that he is about to die. He keeps working anyway.

Afterward, he does not talk much about that day. He tells others only what is necessary. He returns home thinner, quieter, and proud of having endured it. His family praises his courage. He takes a job in fire service a few years later, and the structure suits him. The station gives him rules, equipment, and a brotherhood that feels safer than ordinary life. Emergencies make sense to him in a way that dinner tables and small talk do not. In fires and vehicle extractions, he becomes focused and competent. Other firefighters respect him because he does not freeze.

But over time, the older memories begin attaching themselves to present ones. The smell of diesel mixed with smoke can pull him backward without warning. When a building call comes in and he hears panicked shouting over radios, his chest tightens before he even steps off the truck. At scenes with children, he feels something in him go cold and far away. He notices himself scanning not only for flames and collapse hazards but for snipers, secondary explosions, escape routes no one else seems worried about. He knows, logically, that he is in his own city, not a war zone, yet his body does not seem convinced.

Sleep becomes its own battleground. He wakes at 2 or 3 in the morning soaked in sweat, heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that the room is filling with smoke or that he has left someone behind. Some nights he dreams of the convoy; other nights the dream borrows faces from recent calls and places them in the old explosion. He avoids going back to sleep because he does not want to reenter it. On those nights he sits in the kitchen in the dark, drinking coffee and listening for sounds outside. The next day he is irritable, abrupt with coworkers, ashamed of how quickly anger comes to him.

His marriage does not survive these years. His ex-wife used to tell him that even when he was home, he seemed posted somewhere else. He kept the television on to drown out quiet. He insisted on sitting where he could see the door in restaurants. If she approached him from behind when he was half asleep, he would jerk violently, once swinging an arm before he fully woke. After that he started sleeping on the edge of the bed or on the couch. Eventually they stop trying to explain each other’s silences. The divorce, when it comes, feels to him both painful and unsurprising. He says she deserves someone “more normal,” though the word catches in his throat.

Now, in middle age, he still shows up for shifts and performs well enough that many people would describe him as dependable. He keeps his gear immaculate. He trains younger firefighters carefully, especially about exit routes and what can happen after an initial blast or collapse. He tells himself this is professionalism, and it is, but it is also fear honed into habit. Off duty, his world is narrower. He avoids crowded festivals, fireworks, and news footage from overseas. He rarely attends family gatherings because the noise, questions, and unpredictability wear him down. He feels most at ease in controlled motion—checking equipment, cleaning the apartment, driving at night.

In quieter moments, what troubles him most is not only the terror but the guilt. He thinks of those he could not carry out, the girl with the pot, the driver burning in front of him, colleagues whose names he still recites internally like a private roll call. He has spent years being the one others rely on, yet he lives with the unshakable sense that at the most important moment, he did not do enough. Even now, decades later, a siren in the distance can make his pulse race and his mind return instantly to that road, that blast, that helpless knowledge that disaster can arrive without warning and change the shape of a life in a single second.
